question: What is the main goal of the Essential Drug Programme in public health?

options.A: Ensuring safe and affordable medicines are always available
options.B: Eliminating the need for doctors in rural clinics
options.C: Reducing the overall salaries of hospital pharmacy staff

explanation: You got this! The whole point of the Essential Drug Programme is to make sure vital, quality medicines remain easy to get and affordable for everyone. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why do nurses play such a big role in carrying out the Essential Drug Programme?

options.A: They work exclusively inside administrative pharmacy offices
options.B: They control the international import budgets for pharmaceuticals
options.C: They interact with patients daily and manage bedside drug use
options.D: They are legally licensed to manufacture commercial vaccines

explanation: Spot on! As a nurse, you are right on the frontline—giving medications, tracking supplies, and teaching patients every single day. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h1)

question: What official list guides healthcare workers on which medicines are approved for public health facilities?
explanation: Well done! The Essential Medicines List (EML) contains the carefully selected drugs needed to meet the priority healthcare needs of the community. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h2)

question: Why do clinics keep a 'buffer stock' of essential drugs?

options.A: To fulfill mandatory export quotas for foreign hospitals
options.B: To hide expired medications away from visiting inspectors
options.C: To prevent running out of drugs during unexpected supply delays
options.D: To increase the financial cost of routine patient treatments

explanation: Exactly! Think of buffer stock as your safety net so the clinic never runs dry when shipments are delayed. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h2)

question: Which inventory rule ensures that medicines closer to their expiration date are used first?
explanation: Correct! FEFO (First-Expired, First-Out) helps prevent waste and patient risk by making sure older stock gets used before new deliveries. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h3)

question: You notice some insulin vials have been sitting on a warm desk for hours. What should you do?

options.A: Dilute the warm insulin with sterile water to restore its cold temperature
options.B: Consult the pharmacy or discard the compromised vials according to policy
options.C: Return them immediately to the patient refrigerator without checking
options.D: Administer them quickly before the expiration date arrives next month

explanation: You nailed it. Insulin is sensitive to heat and loses its potency when left out. Always check with pharmacy or follow safety rules rather than risking a patient's dose. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h3)

question: What is the term for giving a patient too many different medications than they actually need?
explanation: Good job! Polypharmacy means 'many drugs' and happens when patients take multiple medications at once, increasing the risk of side effects. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h4)

question: Why is rational drug use so important in the fight against antibiotic resistance?

options.A: It ensures that pharmaceutical companies make higher profits annually
options.B: It guarantees that all drugs are manufactured using local herbs only
options.C: It stops patients from ever visiting a public health facility again
options.D: It prevents the overuse and misuse of antibiotics that cause bacteria to mutate

explanation: Spot on! Using antibiotics wisely stops germs from learning how to beat our drugs. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h4)

question: What is the main goal of supporting a patient with their medication routine for a chronic illness?

options.A: Reducing the workload of the hospital records department
options.B: Forcing the patient to purchase expensive imported vitamins
options.C: Preventing the patient from asking questions about their care
options.D: Helping the patient take medications correctly and consistently

explanation: Correct! Adherence support is all about encouraging and helping patients stick to their treatment plan so they can get better. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h5)

question: A patient with a bacterial infection wants to stop taking antibiotics after two days because they feel fine. What should you tell them?

options.A: They must double the remaining dose on the third day instead
options.B: They should save the remaining pills for a headache next week
options.C: Stopping early can cause the infection to return stronger and more resistant
options.D: It is completely safe to stop once fever symptoms disappear

explanation: You got it! Always encourage patients to finish the full dose so the infection doesn't bounce back stronger. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h5)

question: What is the main focus of 'pharmacovigilance'?

options.A: Transporting bulk cargo across regional borders
options.B: Monitoring and reporting adverse drug reactions
options.C: Setting international market prices for herbal supplements
options.D: Manufacturing sterile equipment for surgical theatres

explanation: Well done! Pharmacovigilance is just a fancy word for watching out for and reporting drug side effects to keep patients safe. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h6)

question: Why are nurse reports on side effects so crucial even after a drug has been approved for sale?

options.A: Drug manufacturers refuse to test their products before public release
options.B: Clinical trials cannot uncover every rare reaction before a drug is sold
options.C: Pharmacists do not notice any patient reactions inside the dispensary
options.D: Hospitals are legally required to fine patients who experience side effects

explanation: Exactly! Pre-market tests are limited, so frontline nurses are vital for catching rare side effects once real people start taking the medication. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h6)

question: Who among the following is NOT typically part of the healthcare team managing essential drugs?
explanation: Easy one! Pilots fly planes, while doctors, nurses, and pharmacists work together to manage patient medications. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h7)

question: How does teamwork between nurses, doctors, and pharmacists improve the Essential Drug Programme?

options.A: By removing the need for any internal hospital quality audits
options.B: By allowing nurses to take over surgical operations from physicians
options.C: By shifting all financial responsibilities entirely onto patients
options.D: By combining different professional skills to prevent drug errors and waste

explanation: Spot on! When healthcare professionals team up, they catch mistakes early and keep patients safe. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h7)
